synthesis.headline: Nor'easter deepens off the Mid-Atlantic while the western trough closes into a Great Basin cutoff — and the ensembles now flatten the mid-latitude West rather than rebuilding the ridge, with amplification retreating to the Canadian Arctic
synthesis.narrative:
The fall longwave dipole that has organized the continent all week is still in place, but both ends have matured. At the eastern end, the coastal cyclone tracked for several days has deepened further — now near 986 mb off the Mid-Atlantic, down from 996 mb a day ago — and remains coupled to a negatively tilted 500 mb shortwave curving through the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic. With the NAO sharply negative (7-day mean near -1.01), this is a trapped, stalling system rather than a progressive one, and WPC expects it to linger off the Northeast before exiting toward the Canadian Maritimes by midweek. At the western end, the deep Pacific Northwest/BC trough of recent days has done what a blocked pattern does: it has detached into a genuine cutoff low over the central Great Basin, with an innermost contour near 564 dam and a cold core of -12 to -14 C over Nevada and Utah, while the ridge has rebuilt to its northwest across the Northwest and western Canada. The geometry — anticyclone displaced northwest of the low rather than stacked poleward of it — is a classically amplified western ridge paired with a cutoff, not a Rex block. Between the two, deep tropical moisture floods the Gulf and Southeast, and a cold front trails from a weak Iowa/Missouri low south into Texas.

Today's centers of action: first, the Nor'easter, driving major multi-cycle coastal flooding, gale-force gusts of 45-65 mph over eastern Long Island and southeastern New England, heavy rain, and a WPC Slight Risk for excessive rainfall over southern New England. Second, the Great Basin cutoff, which will pivot slowly before ejecting east into the Plains midweek; ahead of it, tropical moisture drawn from East Pacific Hurricane Polo sets up a multi-day heavy-rain and flash-flood regime spreading from the Four Corners across the Plains and Mississippi Valley, with mountain snow in the higher terrain — WPC already hangs broad Marginal and embedded Slight Risk excessive-rainfall areas through midweek. Third, Canada carries real weight today: a deep 975 hPa low over the Gulf of Alaska drives a tight wind gradient along the BC coast, while a 1037 hPa high over Hudson Bay reinforces unseasonably cool air across the Prairie provinces, and a separate 987 hPa low near Labrador trails fronts toward the Northeast. In Mexico, Hurricane Polo near Cabo Corrientes is both a direct coastal-impact threat and the moisture source for the Four Corners rains.

Upstairs, the Air Mass RGB ties the eastern story together cleanly: a vivid, compact high-PV dry streamer wraps cyclonically around the Mid-Atlantic cutoff — a credible stratospheric-intrusion signature on its cyclonic flank — while the sharpest airmass boundary, marking the implied jet corridor, runs from the central Plains northeast through the Ohio Valley, separating dry upper air to the northwest from deep green tropical moisture to the southeast. The regime-change test is where today departs from recent framing. Comparing the two ensemble leads directly, both the 6-10 day (Oct 1-5) and 8-14 day (Oct 3-9) means put their dominant positive height anomaly over the Canadian Arctic near Baffin (+6 to +9 dam), not over the western or south-central U.S. The 6-10 day flattens the CONUS toward zonal flow with the zero-anomaly line cutting through the Pacific Northwest and no positive dome over the West; the 8-14 day shows a ridge axis arcing from the Southwest into the Arctic but with western-U.S. anomalies near zero and a deepening east Pacific trough (-6 to -12 dam west of BC). WPC's extended discussion reinforces this, noting guidance has trended toward the lower-amplitude, more split-flow ECMWF camp. In other words, the mid-latitude western ridge is genuinely not regenerating over the lower 48 — the durable, self-repeating block has retreated poleward to the Canadian Arctic while the West flattens and cools. That is a real shift from the "south-central ridge regenerates and endures" outcome the data pointed to a day ago.
synthesis.climate_context: The ONI table's "current" label lags its own data: the equatorial Pacific warmed out of last winter's weak La Niña, crossed positive in spring, and reaches roughly +1.80 by JJA 2026, so late September sits in a moderate-to-strong El Niño, not the labeled cool state. The tropics fit that state and the just-past hurricane-season peak with a textbook basin split — the Atlantic is quiet, with Tropical Storm Gonzalo near the Cabo Verde Islands and Tropical Depression Fay near the Azores both far offshore and no development expected in seven days, while the East Pacific is hyperactive with three simultaneous hurricanes (Polo near Cabo Corrientes, Odalys west-southwest of Baja, Nolo south of the Big Island), a Tehuantepec-area disturbance at 90 percent, and another likely depression east-southeast of Hawaii at 70 percent. The North American Monsoon is fading into its late-season phase but still supplies the Pacific-and-Gulf moisture overlap that, combined with Polo's tropical connection, will feed the Four Corners and Plains rains next week. Late-season severe weather remains in its expected ridge-periphery, southern-Plains mode rather than as deep-Plains outbreaks. Teleconnections are a weak warm-season cross-check but align with the height field: the sharply negative NAO supports the stalling Atlantic cutoff and the emerging high-latitude Arctic block, and the weakly negative PNA is consistent with the retreat of the western ridge.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. SPC carries only a Marginal severe risk for western Oklahoma into northwest Texas late afternoon into early evening, where steep lapse rates and strong deep-layer shear support isolated large hail and severe gusts mainly 22Z-02Z. Beyond the southern New England excessive-rainfall Slight Risk, WPC also flags a Slight Risk over the Middle Mississippi Valley today, with secondary activity developing over the southern Rockies and central/southern High Plains Sunday night into Monday. Florida stays in a wet onshore-flow regime into early October. In Canada, watch the strong BC coastal wind gradient beneath the Gulf of Alaska low and the reinforcing cool push into the Prairies behind the Hudson Bay high.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a deep cyclone centered off the mid-Atlantic coast with a central pressure near 986 mb, surrounded by very tightly packed isobars indicating a steep gradient across the coastal Northeast and western Atlantic — this is the strongest system on the chart and the primary driver of hazardous wind and surf conditions along that coastline. A broad 1027 mb high sits over the upper Great Lakes and Ontario, with its ridge extending southward through the eastern Plains, generating a generally slack gradient across much of the interior East. Across the West, a cluster of weak lows and highs fills the Great Basin and Rockies, pressures ranging roughly 1009 to 1023 mb with gentle gradients, consistent with a diffuse, disorganized pattern there. A cold front extends southward from a low near the Iowa-Missouri border (around 1004 mb) down into Texas and curves toward the Gulf Coast, with a warm front pushing northeast from the same low toward the Great Lakes; the Gulf Coast frontal zone, where dew points in the upper 70s and surface winds are backing ahead of the front, is the clearest focus for moisture convergence and lift on this analysis. A separate stationary or slow-moving frontal segment is visible across the central Rockies and southern Intermountain West, but the slack gradients there limit the implied forcing compared with the Atlantic system and the Plains cold front.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC 00Z Saturday 26 September 2026 surface analysis shows the dominant Canadian feature as a deep low centered near 975 hPa over what appears to be the Gulf of Alaska or the southern Alaska panhandle region, with a well-developed occluded front sweeping southeastward and a trailing cold front pushing into the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia; tightly packed isobars around that system indicate strong gradient winds along the BC coast and into the coastal ranges. Across interior and eastern Canada the pattern is comparatively slack, with a broad 1037 hPa high positioned roughly over Hudson Bay or the eastern Canadian Shield, its anticyclonic circulation producing northerly flow on its western flank that likely reinforces unseasonably cool air across the Prairie provinces. A separate surface low near 987 hPa sits in what appears to be the central northern Atlantic, possibly near Labrador or the Labrador Sea based on the visible coastline geometry, with associated frontal boundaries trailing southwestward toward the northeastern United States. Along the US border, a cold front extends from the Pacific system through the northern Rockies and into the northern Plains states, and the pressure gradient between the Gulf of Alaska low and the Hudson Bay high implies an implied corridor of active post-frontal flow across Alberta and Saskatchewan. In the high Arctic portion of the chart, several labeled lows in the 978 to 1020 hPa range are visible near Greenland and the Canadian Archipelago, consistent with the polar environment and not indicating unusual intensity at those latitudes.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: Valid 1200 UTC 26 September 2026, this 500 mb chart shows a strongly amplified longwave pattern across the contiguous United States. A deep, closed low center is located over the central Great Basin, with the innermost closed contour near 564 dam and the core of the cold anomaly (labeled around -12 to -14 degrees C) extending across Nevada and into Utah; the closure of height contours around this center confirms it is a genuine cutoff, detached from the main westerly flow rather than an open trough translating downstream. To its northwest, a sprawling ridge axis extends across the Pacific Northwest and into western Canada, with heights rising to near 594 dam or above along the ridge core, and this ridge-cutoff dipole configuration — the anticyclone displaced somewhat to the northwest of the low rather than directly poleward at the same longitude — does not meet the strict geometry of a Rex block but represents a classically amplified western ridge paired with a cutoff low, a pattern associated with slow or blocked progression. A surface high is marked over the northern Plains with a surface low labeled in red off the mid-Atlantic coast, consistent with a separate eastern shortwave trough reflected in the 579-580 dam contours curving through the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic; that eastern feature shows a slight negative tilt. Across the southern tier from Texas eastward through the Gulf States, heights are relatively high (588-594 dam) with weak, nearly zonal flow and only modest wind barbs, while the implied jet corridor wraps cyclonically around the cutoff low's southern and eastern flanks through the central Rockies and Plains. Overall the pattern is blocked rather than progressive, with the cutoff low expected to pivot slowly rather than translate, and the eastern trough secondary and downstream of the dominant western closed system.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 26 September 2026 at 1321Z shows a broad green airmass dominating the Gulf of Mexico and the southeastern United States, indicating deep tropical moisture extending northward through the Mississippi Valley and into the mid-Atlantic region. A prominent dry intrusion, appearing as a vivid orange-brown streamer, wraps cyclonically around what appears to be a closed upper-level feature centered near the Mid-Atlantic coast, with the streamer's leading edge curling southward along the Eastern Seaboard — the compact, elongated geometry and saturated orange coloring on the cyclonic flank are consistent with a stratospheric intrusion signature. The sharpest airmass boundary, implying the likely jet corridor, runs from roughly the central Plains diagonally northeast through the Ohio Valley, separating drier reddish upper-tropospheric air to the northwest from the moist green air to the southeast. In the southwestern Atlantic and Caribbean, two organized convective clusters with cold white tops are visible east of Florida and near the Greater Antilles, both embedded within the moist green airmass. The western contiguous United States displays broad reddish-orange tones consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under a ridge, but the diffuse, extensive nature of that coloring argues against a stratospheric intrusion there.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1310Z on 26 September 2026 shows a broad green belt of tropical moist air spanning the ITCZ from the eastern Pacific through Central America and into the Atlantic, with numerous bright white convective clusters embedded along it, most visually prominent just west of Central America and over the far eastern Pacific where a tightly organized white swirl near the left edge of the disk suggests a tropical cyclone or well-developed tropical low. A second area of organized deep convection sits near the eastern Pacific coast of Mexico, with additional scattered convective cells across equatorial South America and the western Amazon basin. The orange-red tones dominating the subtropical Pacific and Atlantic on both flanks of the tropics represent dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air consistent with the subtropical ridge regime expected in late September rather than stratospheric intrusions. Across Canada and the northern tier, a sharp transition from the tropical green airmass to cooler, darker blue-green tones marks the polar airmass boundary, with several comma-shaped cloud systems visible off the northeastern U.S. coast and over the western North Atlantic, implying active baroclinic systems along the storm track. In the Southern Hemisphere, a series of curving cloud bands with orange-streaked wrapping in the far south of the domain, near the tip of South America, indicates active extratropical cyclone activity consistent with the Southern Ocean westerlies.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking feature is the very high probability of above-normal temperatures across the eastern third of the country, with the 90-100% confidence tier covering most of the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and New England coastline, and the 80-90% tier extending into the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes region — an exceptionally strong signal for a CPC outlook at this range. A broad above-normal signal also covers California and much of the Intermountain West, with probabilities generally in the 60-70% range and a tighter 70-80% core over coastal Southern California. The central Plains and upper Midwest fall into the near-normal category, forming a meridionally oriented corridor from the Dakotas through Kansas that separates the two above-normal lobes, which is consistent with a trough axis near the central Rockies or High Plains keeping that zone relatively neutral while ridging dominates both coasts. The geometry of dual coastal ridging with an intervening near-normal axis implies the forecast models are maintaining a persistent amplified upper-level pattern through the October 1-5 period rather than projecting a progressive or zonal breakdown. In Alaska the signal is split, with below-normal probabilities in the western portion and above-normal along the southern coast, consistent with a different regime governing that region independently of the Lower 48 pattern.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height anomaly forecast, valid October 1-5, 2026, made September 25, 2026. Heights are plotted in solid green contours at 60 m intervals, with anomalies in dashed red (positive) and dashed blue (negative).

The dominant feature is a strong positive height anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic, roughly centered near the Queen Elizabeth Islands or northern Baffin Bay area, where the red dashed contours suggest a positive departure on the order of +6 to +9 dam above normal; this corresponds to the ridge axis extending from that Arctic high southward into central Canada, with the 552 dam contour bulging well poleward. Over western North America, the positive anomaly signal is comparatively weak or absent — the zero-anomaly line (the boundary between red and blue dashed contours) appears to cut through roughly the Pacific Northwest or British Columbia coast, meaning any western ridge amplification has largely retreated; there is no clear positive anomaly dome sitting over the U.S. West Coast or Great Basin. A negative anomaly region is evident over the north-central Pacific and separately implied by blue dashed contours over Alaska and the western Aleutians, consistent with a trough in that sector. The height contours across the contiguous United States from roughly the Rockies eastward run in a relatively flat, west-to-west-northwest orientation, and with the positive anomaly concentrated far north in the Arctic rather than over western CONUS, the pattern implies a trend toward more zonal flow across the mid-latitudes of the lower 48, with the primary amplification having shifted poleward rather than holding over western North America.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This image is a 500 mb height and height-departure (anomaly) forecast, not a pure anomaly chart — the green solid contours are absolute heights at 60 dam intervals and the dashed contours are the departures. The dominant feature is a deep, positively tilted trough over the eastern North Pacific, with tightly packed contours and the implied flow strongly amplified; the ridge-trough pattern shows a broad ridge axis running roughly from the southwestern United States northeastward into the central Canadian Arctic, with the 576–582 dam contours arching well into the high latitudes rather than being confined to the Southwest or northern Mexico. Over western Canada and the northern Rockies the heights appear near or slightly above 570–576 dam, and the blue dashed anomaly contours in that sector are near the zero line or weakly negative, suggesting little positive departure there; the more pronounced positive anomaly center, indicated by the red dashed contours, appears to be located over the central Canadian Arctic near Baffin Island, where departures read on the order of +6 to +9 dam above normal. The eastern Pacific trough carries a negative anomaly of roughly -6 to -12 dam west of the British Columbia coast, consistent with an unseasonably deep mean trough at that position, while the contour gradient across the western U.S. is relatively relaxed, arguing against a strong ridge core over the northern Rockies or northern Plains during the valid period of 3–9 October 2026.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Strong nor'easter off Mid-Atlantic coast will bring major coastal flooding through multiple high tide cycles this weekend, with widespread inundation expected by Saturday morning high tide. Significant coastal impacts include rip currents, beach erosion, and property damage extending to Southern New England through Monday. Strong to gale-force winds gusting 45-65 mph across Eastern Long Island and Southeastern New England will cause power outages and tree damage. Heavy rain from Northern New Jersey into Southern New England may produce localized flash flooding, particularly in urban areas and small streams. Slight Risk issued for excessive rainfall Southern New England Saturday-Sunday and Middle Mississippi Valley Saturday. Secondary activity expected Southern Rockies, Southern High Plains, and Central Plains Sunday evening into Monday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Marginal severe risk for western Oklahoma into northwest Texas late afternoon into early evening. Upper trough and jet stream feature moving northeast across the southern Plains with lee trough maintaining southerly low-level flow. Scattered to widespread thunderstorm development expected around 21-23 UTC as steep lapse rates and erosion of MLCINH occur by mid-afternoon. Strong deep-layer shear will support storm organization with isolated threats for large hail and severe gusts mainly 22z-02z. Elsewhere, conditions remain quiescent for severe weather.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale discussions. The Storm Prediction Center is not currently monitoring any organized convective threat requiring detailed mesoscale analysis.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: Tropical Storm Gonzalo near Cabo Verde Islands and Tropical Depression Fay west-southwest of Azores under NHC advisories. No tropical cyclone formation expected in next seven days.

East Pacific: Three active hurricanes—Polo near Cabo Corrientes Mexico, Odalys west-southwest of southern Baja California, and Nolo south of Hawaii's Big Island. Organizing low pressure south of Gulf of Tehuantepec expected to develop into tropical depression within one to two days, moving west-northwest parallel to Mexican coast (90% seven-day formation probability). Separate broad low pressure developing 1000 miles east-southeast of Hawaiian Islands likely to form depression early-to-mid next week, moving northeast away from islands (70% seven-day formation probability).

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a transition from weak La Niña conditions in late 2025 (NDJ anomaly -0.60) toward El Niño by mid-2026. The shift accelerates through spring, crossing neutral territory around February-March 2026. By summer 2026, El Niño strengthens considerably, with the JJA anomaly reaching +1.80, indicating moderate to strong conditions. This represents a clear phase flip from current cool to warm waters over the next six months.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative (-0.34), little changed over the past week, with no strong directional signal. AO has swung positive (+0.53) after several days near or below zero, also showing no clear trend. NAO has fallen noticeably negative (-0.66), dropping from -0.51 last week, with a 7-day mean of -1.01. The NAO decline is the most notable feature; negative NAO can support retention of eastern North American troughs. Summer teleconnection patterns are inherently weak, so these should be viewed as directional support rather than definitive signals.
